extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in religion, satire, and social criticism (readers of Mark Twain)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th/early-20th-century satirical essay that evaluates the doctrines, practices, and literature of Christian Science and related faith-cure movements, offering literary and practical criticisms. The piece mixes humor, anecdote, and argument to show what the author sees as defects in doctrine, style, and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present evidence when claiming 'I have Proved'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Without ever presenting anything which may rightfully be called by the strong name of Evidence, and sometimes without even mentioning a reason for a deduction at all, it thunders out the startling words, 'I have Proved' so and so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of proof must be accompanied by actual evidence and reasons. Anti-pattern: authoritative assertions ('I have Proved') delivered with no supporting data or argument. Example criticism: the Christian Science book asserts proofs while providing no evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simplicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of an obscure, involved style: phrases such as "labored and tumultuous, and in places violent, that the treatment was involved and erratic, and almost, as a rule, bewildering; that to lack of simplicity was added a lack of vocabulary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain, orderly exposition; avoid convoluted, tumultuous, or needlessly ornate phrasing that leaves readers bewildered. Anti-pattern: writing that relies on rhythm or grandiosity instead of clear meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute, universal claims of cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that some sects "claim ability to cure every conceivable human ailment through the application of their mental forces alone" and that this look[s] "like claiming too much."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from blanket promises of universal efficacy. Modest, testable claims build confidence; overreaching promises are dangerous and undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not forbid complementary medical treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: "The Faith Cure and the Prayer Cure probably do no harm when they do no good, since they do not forbid the patient to help out the cure with medicines; but the others bar medicines, and claim ability to cure every conceivable human ailment... There would seem to be an element of danger here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow patients access to conventional medical care alongside mental/faith-based approaches. Anti-pattern: forbidding all medicines while claiming exclusive healing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between metaphysical claims and practical behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony: "Nothing exists but Mind? ... I gave her an imaginary check, and now she is suing me for substantial dollars. It looks inconsistent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal assertions about the unreality of matter should be reflected (or at least not contradicted) in everyday practices. Avoid claiming metaphysical nonexistence while engaging in routine material transactions that presuppose material reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'showy incoherences' and oracular jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: The book "pours out the book's showy incoherences... listening to a lively and aggressive and oracular speech delivered in an unknown tongue... whose spirit you get but not the particulars."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute pompous, repetitive jargon or oracular pronouncements for clear, substantive argument. Anti-pattern: devotees reciting jargon verbatim without originating thought or explanatory content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address logical implications and internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's puzzle: if "there is no such thing as matter, how can matter propagate things?" and other internal difficulties of the doctrine are left insufficiently explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theory should account for its own implications and answer straightforward logical objections. Anti-pattern: sweeping assertions that leave obvious explanatory questions unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage appropriately with physical symptoms; do not dismiss bodily signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner refuses to accept tongue, pulse, or patient's expressions of pain: "We deal with the mind only, not with its dumb servants... There is no such thing as feeling: therefore, to speak of a non-existent thing as existent is a contradiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsible healers should consider physical signs and patient reports rather than categorically dismissing them as mere illusion. Anti-pattern: wholesale denial of bodily evidence and refusal to perform basic examination or diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify claims of divine revelation or prophetic fulfillment
rubrics_metrics.description: Healer interprets Revelation to identify the movement's founder: quoting Revelation xii and declaring the founder plainly indicated; Twain treats this as a dubious proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that a doctrine or person fulfills prophecy require rigorous justification rather than casual or forced scriptural readings. Anti-pattern: reading symbolic texts as literal, decisive proof without independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: avoid complacent self-satisfaction and apodictical absolutism
rubrics_metrics.description: The book's "serenities of self-satisfaction" and reliance on an "Apodictical Principle" produce a "limitless confidence and complacency" that is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain intellectual humility; avoid presenting beliefs as absolutely beyond question. Anti-pattern: dogmatic, triumphant rhetoric that discourages scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict claims to domains where the method demonstrably works
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's recommendation: "In my opinion it ought to let diseases alone and confine itself to surgery. There it would have everything its own way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit practices to areas with demonstrable efficacy; prefer narrow, supported applications rather than sweeping endeavor. Example: if a technique reliably helps with certain surgical recoveries, emphasize that rather than asserting panacean powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the power of imagination/faith but acknowledge ethical risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain notes the potency of the patient's imagination (placebo effects, royal touch, relic cures) but warns that when faith-based cures forbid other aid they become dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge placebo/imagination effects and use them ethically (as adjuncts), not as reasons to prohibit other effective care. Anti-pattern: exploiting psychological effects while denying or suppressing medical alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a respectful and judicial tone when criticizing technical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Postscript confession about harshly condemning a scientific tract on encephalic anatomy: the author regrets starting with scorn instead of a judicial spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should evaluate with respect and care; avoid letting initial sarcasm or temperament produce unfair or unjudicial denunciations. Example: the author corrected his prior intemperate review upon reflection.
